newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open higher before Sept payroll data.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open higher before Sept payroll data.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries opened higher on Friday ahead of the closely watched U.S. employment report for September.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year Treasury bond was up 9/32 to 99-5/32, yielding 6.82 percent, in early trade. The two-year Treasury note rose 1/32 to 100-1/32, yielding 5.98 percent.

"The market is betting on a favorable payrolls number," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A. "There was some profit-taking yesterday, but the bias still is that it will be a supportive number."
Stiles cited buying in the middle of the curve overnight.
Kim Rupert, senior economist at MMS International, pointed to buying overnight in both Tokyo and London as setting a positive tone at the open in New York.
"The market expects a friendly employment report and people don't want to get caught behind this rally, so we're getting a little bit of a bid right now," said Rupert.
Economists polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that payrolls expanded by 166,000 new jobs in September.
The question is whether a payroll number near 170,000 new jobs or so will be weak enough to lift the market further.
"I don't know if a number like 170,000 or 175,000 does a lot for the market anymore," said Stiles.
"Job growth of 170,000 to 175,000 has largely been discounted," said Rupert. "It will depend on the rest of the mix, like hourly earnings and the unemployment rate."

But Rupert said if the market dips, it will find buyers because people are convinced -- both by recent data and by the Federal Reserve's decision to keep rates steady -- that the economy has begun to slow.
"People want to buy this market," she said. "They think the Fed can maybe stay on hold through the rest of the year."
If the September employment report comes in near expectations, it will confirm the wisdom of the Fed's decision to leave rates unchanged at its most recent policy meeting.
The government will report September nonfarm payrolls and the monthly jobless rate at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
The 166,000 September job growth forecast compares to 250,000 new jobs created in August and more than 200,000 each month since May.
The unemployment rate is forecast to have risen to 5.2 percent. August's reading of 5.1 percent marked the lowest jobless rate since March of 1989 when it stood at 5.0 percent.
Analysts said fewer local government hirings -- mainly of teachers -- and a cooling in manufacturing probably restrained jobs growth in September.
In early trade, three-month bill rates were up one basis point to 4.91 percent. Six-month bills were unchanged at 5.10 percent.
Five-year notes were up 4/32 to 100-8/32, yielding 6.32 percent. Ten-year notes were up 8/32 to 103-3/32, yielding 6.56 percent.
-- North American Treasury Desk 212-859-1679
